comments.text:
~ Rock, Paper, Scissors ~

I keep going back to the idea that AI could just be a kind of vehicle for the WEF/Build-Back-Better/Electrify-Society narrative and/or agenda. Fair enough I guess...

I sometimes read the comments under You Tube videos that talk about AI and there are often many good points that the human collective raise against AI, some rather amusing.

Even if AI has all the info in the world or even the universe, and even if it can see, hear, smell and taste, it's still wrapped and trapped in its ultra-layers-cocoon of technology, of metal, plastic, rare-earths and large-scale electrical grids and nuclear power plants-- all at once removed, yet completely within, the contexts of Earth and its natural whims, like earthquakes, floods, hurricanes, volcanoes, asteriod impacts, mudslides, weather and continental subduction...

Maybe my puny human mind simply cannot conceive of what AI will have in mind for its own future. But AI will always be constrained by the laws of physics. In the face of those, AI's own intelligence, whatever it will become, will only go so far too and, like humans, have its own glaring disadvantages that may increasingly become apparent, maybe painfully so, as/if civilization grinds down.

Rock, paper, scissors: Your move, HAL...

My 'yardstick' for whenever anyone (but so frequently that someone is Sam Altman) talks about how AI will change everyone's life (or in this case, substitute in "economically valuable work" (by what definition of 'valuable' ??)) is to think about how (or when) it might benefit the kids who survive by combing the rubbish dumps in Bangladesh.  (Because of a really sobering documentary that stuck with me).

The GDP output might be a rounding error, but I guarantee that these kids spend many more hours in economically productive work than Altman's perception of the average person.

So sure, I'm personally gonna be very appreciative of the impact this research AI bot will have on my life, starting immediately.  

But! never lose sight of how far away the tech is from making life even infinitesimally better (i.e meaningfully impacts the time-value equation) for an almost unimaginably large number of the worlds most situationally disadvantaged.

comments.author: @MistressBlah
comments.text:
So, the thing about these types of jobs that it "might" automate, is that the work still requires us humans to sit and think about these things for a while. I don't think these numbers are right because of exactly that. As an engineer, I can see this doing some parts of my job, but at best it's going to allow me to just think more. To be more comfortable with the decisions I am making. It's really difficult to quantify what more time really ends up doing. 

Humans are not perfect creatures. And the manner in which the figures given for automating labor are shown seem to think that. Bottom line is, if Deep Research thinks it's supposedly saving me 5 hours on a research task, what I ultimately lose is the time to just sit with the task. 

Think about all those times you've gone to research something and ended with more than what you though you were looking for.

I do think there is good value in this, but as nothing more than a better search engine.
